title: Stress Recovery During Exposure to Natural and Urban Environments. Journal of Environmental Psychology. 11: 201-230
research_question: To investigate the extent to which exposure to different everyday outdoor environments may foster or hinder recovery from stress, and to test if natural settings promote greater stress recovery than urban environments, with differences evident in emotional states and physiological indicators.

participants.description: 60 males and 60 females, undergraduate volunteers at the University of Delaware, studying in diverse fields.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Stressor: 10-minute black and white videotape ('It Didn't Have to Happen') depicting work accidents with simulated blood and mutilation.

Recovery: 10-minute color/sound videotapes of six different everyday outdoor settings. Two natural settings (Vegetation, Water) and four urban settings (Heavy traffic, Light traffic, Many pedestrians, Few pedestrians).

measures.construct: Self-reported affective states (Fear, Positive Affects, Anger/Aggression, Attentiveness/Interest, Sadness)

mechanisms: Nature responses have a salient parasympathetic nervous system component
Nature fosters a shift towards a more positively-toned emotional state
Nature leads to positive changes in physiological activity levels
Quick-onset positive affective reactions to nature play a central role
Biological preparedness for positive responses to unthreatening nature
Urban environments may elicit appraisals of slight risk or tension, leading to mild sympathetic mobilization
Content differences (natural vs. human-made properties) are decisive in accounting for differences in recovery and intake/attention, rather than variations in stimulation levels.
implementation_implications: Short-duration nature exposures (several seconds to minutes) may have an important function for urbanites in facilitating recovery from daily stressors.
Environmental stress research should broaden beyond stressors to include concern for settings that facilitate recovery.

tables.description: Environments displayed during stress recovery period, detailing visual content and sounds for each of the six settings (Nature Vegetation, Nature Water, Urban Heavy traffic, Urban Light traffic, Urban Many pedestrians, Urban Few pedestrians).

Influences of environments on affective states: factor score changes from pre- to post-recovery for ZIPERS factors (Fear, Anger/Aggression, Positive Affects, Sadness, Attentiveness/Interest) across Nature, Pedestrian mall, and Traffic environments.

limitations: Results cannot be generalized directly to longer term nature exposures involving active participation (e.g., wilderness backpacking).
Heart monitoring methods did not allow precise disentanglement of parasympathetic and sympathetic influences.
No objective procedures were available for measuring information rate of non-static, audiovisual environmental displays.
Verbal judgments of information rate after 10-minute video simulation may be misleading due to habituation.
Temporal non-congruence of measurement modes (self-report vs. physiological) limited correlation analysis to longer-term relationships.
